name: Shaka kaSenzangakhona
note:
A room built from two incompatible archives. Shaka left no writings — the Zulu had no script in his lifetime — so everything here was written down by someone else. The izibongo are Zulu praise-poetry, composed by imbongi and carried orally for a century before being transcribed. The travellers' accounts are two young English traders at Port Natal with commercial interests in the outcome. Nathaniel Isaacs wrote to Henry Fynn advising him to make the chiefs out as bloodthirsty as he could, because it would help their case and sell better; that letter survives. Most of the Shaka the world knows comes down through it. The room holds both archives and says which is which.

A NOTE ADDED ON REPAIR. Three works on this shelf were missing and have been rebuilt from Isaacs's 1836 *Travels and Adventures in Eastern Africa*, which is public domain. **One of them was previously titled as Fynn and is not:** Fynn's diary survives in James Stuart's 1950 edited compilation, whose editorial layer is not clearly out of copyright, so it is not held here. Fynn is present throughout Isaacs's account as his companion — but these are Isaacs's words, and given that Isaacs is the one who wrote the letter about making the chiefs bloodthirsty, the difference matters.

works.title: uDlungwana kaNdaba
works.source: Zulu izibongo, transcribed from oral tradition
works.note: The opening praise-names. Shaka is addressed by what he did, not by title — the form of Zulu praise-poetry, in which a man is named by his acts.

works.title: The Praise of the Spear
works.source: Zulu izibongo, transcribed from oral tradition
works.note: The iklwa, the short stabbing spear that replaced the thrown assegai, praised in the poems as the thing that changed war.

works.title: The Imbongi Speaks
works.source: Zulu izibongo, transcribed from oral tradition
works.note: On the office of the praise-singer itself: the imbongi could praise and could also rebuke, and was the one voice permitted to do both.

works.title: At Shaka's Court — Isaacs, Vol. I ch. XI
works.source: Nathaniel Isaacs, *Travels and Adventures in Eastern Africa, descriptive of the Zoolus, their manners, customs, etc.* · London, E. Churton, 1836 · Internet Archive · public domain
works.note: The European account of Shaka's court. **A CORRECTION TO THIS SHELF:** this text is Isaacs, not Fynn. Henry Fynn's diary was compiled and edited by James Stuart and published in 1950; that edition's editorial work is not clearly out of copyright, so it is not reproduced here. Fynn appears in these pages constantly — he was Isaacs's companion at Port Natal — but the words are Isaacs's. Read against the izibongo, not instead of them.

works.title: The Government of the Zoolas — Isaacs, Vol. II ch. XVI
works.source: Nathaniel Isaacs, *Travels and Adventures in Eastern Africa, descriptive of the Zoolus, their manners, customs, etc.* · London, E. Churton, 1836 · Internet Archive · public domain
works.note: Isaacs describing Zulu government, law and custom for an English readership — and the chapter to hold against his own surviving letter to Fynn, urging him to make the chiefs out as bloodthirsty as he could because it would sell. **The letter is not in this book and Isaacs did not intend it to be read beside this chapter.** The distortion is part of the record and the room says so.

works.title: The Death of Chaka — Isaacs, Vol. I ch. XVIII–XIX
works.source: Nathaniel Isaacs, *Travels and Adventures in Eastern Africa, descriptive of the Zoolus, their manners, customs, etc.* · London, E. Churton, 1836 · Internet Archive · public domain
works.note: Isaacs on the killing at kwaDukuza, September 1828, by Shaka's half-brothers — and then his summary of the man, whose 'vices and atrocities seem nearly without a parallel'. **That sentence is the one that travelled.** Most of what the world came to believe about Shaka descends from this chapter and the ones around it. The Zulu tradition on this shelf disagrees about almost everything except that he died.
